key_insight: Single-crystal Ti-15Mo shows an unexpected inversion of cubic elastic anisotropy, with orientations near <111> being the softest in both indentation modulus and yield onset, and its yield response cannot be explained by simple CRSS/Schmid-factor models.
engineering_relevance: Texture and grain orientation can strongly alter local stiffness and yield in Ti-15Mo, so processing routes for β-titanium components should account for orientation-dependent nanomechanical behavior rather than relying on isotropic or Schmid-only design rules.
method: EBSD was combined with nanoindentation to target grains with surface normals near <111>, <124>, <011>, <023>, and <013>.
Measured indentation modulus, hardness, strain-rate sensitivity, and yield onset were compared across orientations.
Strain-rate-jump tests were used to estimate activation volumes and infer likely deformation mechanisms.
evidence_signal: Across the tested orientations, indentation modulus varied by about 10%, yield onset by 41%, and hardness by 6.6%, with activation volumes of 18–31 b^3 suggesting kink-pair-nucleation-controlled plasticity.
watch_item: The interpretation relies on nanoindentation and model comparisons on a limited set of orientations, so mechanism attribution and the proposed retained ω explanation should be validated with complementary microstructural evidence.
paper_title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions
